title: What are Flink restart strategies — fixed-delay (retry N times with a delay), failure-rate (allow N failures within an interval), exponential-delay (increasing backoff), and no-restart — and how do you configure them (RestartStrategies.fixedDelayRestart(attempts, delay))?

s1_definition.profdef: A Flink restart strategy defines how the job should recover when a failure causes it to fail, controlling whether and how many times Flink restarts the job and with what delay between attempts. Fixed-delay restarts the job a fixed number of times, waiting a constant delay between attempts. Failure-rate allows the job to keep restarting as long as the number of failures within a sliding time interval stays below a threshold, failing permanently only if failures become too frequent. Exponential-delay restarts with a backoff that grows after each failure up to a maximum, which avoids hammering a struggling dependency. No-restart fails the job immediately on the first failure. These are configured either in the job via the RestartStrategies API or globally in the cluster configuration.
s1_definition.analogy: When a processing clerk at the National Bank of India stumbles and drops the whole tray, the branch manager must decide how to react. Fixed-delay is like saying "pick it up and try again, wait thirty seconds between tries, and you get three tries total." Failure-rate is like saying "keep trying as long as you don't stumble more than three times in any ten-minute window; if you do, something is seriously wrong, so stop." Exponential-delay is like saying "try again after one minute, then if it fails again wait two minutes, then four, giving the jammed machine time to recover." No-restart is like saying "if you drop the tray even once, stop everything and call me." Each policy matches a different judgment about how to handle repeated trouble.
s1_definition.oneliner: Restart strategies decide whether and how Flink retries a failed job: fixed-delay for constant retries, failure-rate for a tolerance window, exponential-delay for growing backoff, and no-restart to fail fast.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Flink restart strategy defines how the job should recover when a failure causes it to fail, controlling whether and how many times Flink restarts the job and with what delay between attempts. Fixed-delay restarts the job a fixed number of times, waiting a constant delay between attempts. Failure-rate allows the job to keep restarting as long as the number of failures within a sliding time interval stays below a threshold, failing permanently only if failures become too frequent. Exponential-delay restarts with a backoff that grows after each failure up to a maximum, which avoids hammering a struggling dependency. No-restart fails the job immediately on the first failure. These are configured either in the job via the RestartStrategies API or globally in the cluster configuration.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When a processing clerk at the National Bank of India stumbles and drops the whole tray, the branch manager must decide how to react. Fixed-delay is like saying "pick it up and try again, wait thirty seconds between tries, and you get three tries total." Failure-rate is like saying "keep trying as long as you don't stumble more than three times in any ten-minute window; if you do, something is seriously wrong, so stop." Exponential-delay is like saying "try again after one minute, then if it fails again wait two minutes, then four, giving the jammed machine time to recover." No-restart is like saying "if you drop the tray even once, stop everything and call me." Each policy matches a different judgment about how to handle repeated trouble.

**One line to remember:** Restart strategies decide whether and how Flink retries a failed job: fixed-delay for constant retries, failure-rate for a tolerance window, exponential-delay for growing backoff, and no-restart to fail fast.

sections.s2_technical:
When a task fails, perhaps because of an exception, a lost task manager, or a transient dependency error, Flink consults the configured restart strategy to decide what to do. With checkpointing enabled, a restart means Flink restores the job from the last completed checkpoint and resumes, so a restart is not a data-loss event; it is a recovery. Without checkpointing, the default strategy is no-restart, which is one reason enabling checkpointing is essential for production.

Fixed-delay is the simplest. You configure it with `RestartStrategies.fixedDelayRestart(3, Time.seconds(10))`, meaning up to three restart attempts with a constant ten-second delay between each. If the job keeps failing past the attempt count, Flink gives up and the job fails terminally. This suits transient issues that usually clear quickly, like a brief network blip. Its weakness is that a constant delay can hammer a dependency that needs longer to recover, and a small attempt count can exhaust quickly during an outage.

Failure-rate is more forgiving for long-running jobs. You configure it with the maximum failures per interval, the measuring interval, and the delay, for example `RestartStrategies.failureRateRestart(3, Time.minutes(5), Time.seconds(10))`, meaning the job may restart freely as long as it does not fail more than three times within any five-minute window; if it does, it fails terminally. This recognizes that an occasional failure over a long lifetime is normal, while a burst of failures signals a real problem that restarting will not fix. Exponential-delay, available as `RestartStrategies.exponentialDelayRestart(...)` with an initial backoff, a multiplier, a maximum backoff, and a reset threshold, increases the wait after each consecutive failure up to a cap and resets once the job has run healthily for a while. This is ideal when the failures come from an overloaded external system, because increasing backoff gives that system room to recover instead of a constant retry storm. No-restart, `RestartStrategies.noRestart()`, fails immediately, which is appropriate for batch jobs where a failure should surface at once or where an external orchestrator handles retries.

The senior nuances: you can set the strategy per job in the execution environment or globally in the cluster config with keys like `restart-strategy` and its parameters, and the per-job setting overrides the cluster default. The restart strategy only governs full-job or region restarts; it works together with the failover strategy, which decides how much of the graph to restart. Choosing a strategy is about the failure's nature: use exponential-delay for flaky external dependencies, failure-rate for long-lived streaming jobs that should tolerate rare blips but stop on sustained failure, fixed-delay for simple transient recovery, and no-restart when an outer system owns retries. You must also make sure the restart does not mask a real bug, so you alert on restart counts, because a job that is silently restarting every minute is as broken as one that is down.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a long-lived fraud-scoring stream job. It occasionally hits a transient failure, such as a brief loss of a task manager or a momentary network glitch to Kafka, and it should recover automatically from its last checkpoint. But if it starts failing repeatedly in a short window, that signals a real defect or a broken dependency, and endlessly restarting would just churn. This is exactly the failure-rate strategy: tolerate rare blips, fail terminally on a burst.

Problem 2 — A different job writes to an external settlement API that sometimes gets overloaded and rejects requests for a while. Retrying immediately at a constant rate would pile on more load and prolong the outage. The job should back off increasingly after each failure to give the API room to recover. This is exactly the exponential-delay strategy.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that models the four strategies deciding whether to restart after a sequence of failures. We define a `Failure` with a timestamp. A `RestartStrategy` interface exposes a method that, given the history of failures, decides whether to restart and how long to wait. We implement `FixedDelayStrategy`, `FailureRateStrategy`, `ExponentialDelayStrategy`, and `NoRestartStrategy`. A `JobSupervisor` feeds a sequence of failures to a chosen strategy and logs each decision. A `RestartStrategyDemo` main class runs a burst of failures through all four strategies and prints how each responds, showing fixed-delay exhausting its attempts, failure-rate giving up after too many failures in the window, exponential-delay increasing its backoff, and no-restart stopping immediately.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  restart-strategy: failure-rate            # fixed-delay | failure-rate | exponential-delay | none
  restart-strategy.failure-rate:
    max-failures-per-interval: 3
    failure-rate-interval: 5 min
    delay: 10 s
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five failures occurring at zero, twenty, forty, sixty, and eighty seconds, run through the four strategies.

Step 1, Fixed-delay with three attempts: The first failure consults the strategy, zero attempts used so far, under the limit, so it restarts with a ten-second delay. The second and third failures also restart with ten-second delays. On the fourth failure, three attempts have been used, so the strategy fails terminally. Fixed-delay stops after exhausting its attempt budget regardless of timing.

Step 2, Failure-rate allowing three per five minutes: The first three failures all fall within the five-minute window but stay at or below three, so each restarts with a ten-second delay. The fourth failure makes four failures in the window, exceeding the limit of three, so the strategy fails terminally. Failure-rate tolerated the blips until the burst crossed the threshold.

Step 3, Exponential-delay: The first failure restarts after one second, the initial backoff. The second restarts after two seconds, the third after four seconds, the fourth after eight seconds, each doubling, and it never fails terminally in this demo because exponential-delay keeps trying with growing patience up to its cap of sixty seconds.

Step 4, No-restart: The very first failure consults the strategy, which always returns terminal, so the job fails immediately on failure number one without any restart.

Step 5: The contrast across strategies is now visible from the logs. Fixed-delay and failure-rate both eventually fail terminally but for different reasons, attempt count versus rate in a window. Exponential-delay keeps recovering with increasing backoff, ideal for a flaky dependency. No-restart fails fast.

Step 6: The demo makes clear how to match a strategy to a situation. For a long-lived streaming job that should survive rare blips but stop on a sustained problem, failure-rate fits. For failures caused by an overloaded external system, exponential-delay's growing backoff avoids a retry storm. For simple transient recovery, fixed-delay suffices, and for batch jobs where an outer orchestrator owns retries, no-restart is right.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Failure occurs → JobSupervisor.onFailure(f)
    │
    ▼
  RestartStrategy.decide(history, current)
    │
    ├─ fixed-delay       ──→ attempts < N ? delay : TERMINAL
    │
    ├─ failure-rate      ──→ failures in interval <= max ? delay : TERMINAL
    │
    ├─ exponential-delay ──→ delay = init * mult^consecutive (capped), keep trying
    │
    └─ no-restart        ──→ TERMINAL immediately
    │
    ▼
  decision >= 0 ? restore from last checkpoint, wait delay, RESTART
  decision <  0 ? job FAILS terminally → alert on-call
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Flink restart strategy defines whether and how the job recovers when a failure causes it to fail, and because a restart with checkpointing enabled means Flink restores from the last completed checkpoint and resumes, choosing the right strategy is about handling repeated trouble sensibly, not about data loss. There are four. Fixed-delay restarts the job up to a configured number of attempts with a constant delay between each, which you set with fixedDelayRestart giving the attempts and the delay; it suits transient issues that clear quickly, but a constant delay can hammer a slow-recovering dependency and the attempt budget can exhaust during a longer outage. Failure-rate lets the job restart freely as long as the number of failures within a sliding interval stays below a threshold, failing terminally only when failures become too frequent; this is ideal for long-lived streaming jobs, because it tolerates the occasional blip that is normal over a long lifetime while stopping on a genuine burst that restarting will not cure.

Exponential-delay increases the backoff after each consecutive failure up to a maximum and resets once the job runs healthily for a while, which is exactly what you want when the failures come from an overloaded external system, because the growing wait gives that system room to recover instead of a constant retry storm. No-restart fails immediately on the first failure, which fits batch jobs where a failure should surface at once, or situations where an external orchestrator owns retries. You configure these either per job through the execution environment's restart-strategy API, which overrides the cluster default, or globally in the cluster configuration, and the restart strategy works together with the failover strategy that decides how much of the graph to restart.

At the National Bank of India I matched strategies to the job's nature. Our long-lived fraud-scoring stream used failure-rate, allowing a few failures within a five-minute window so that a brief task-manager loss or a momentary Kafka glitch recovered automatically from the last checkpoint, but a burst of failures in a short window failed the job terminally and paged the on-call engineer, because that signals a real defect that churning restarts would only hide. A separate job that wrote to an occasionally-overloaded settlement API used exponential-delay, so that when the API started rejecting requests the job backed off with increasing delays and stopped piling load onto a struggling dependency. We also alerted on restart counts, because a job quietly restarting every minute is just as broken as one that is down, only harder to notice. Being able to name the four strategies, explain the configuration API, and above all reason about which failure nature calls for which policy, while stressing that you must monitor restarts so recovery does not mask a bug, is exactly the operational judgment an interviewer is listening for.
